findings.title: Password check skipped whenever totpCode is non-empty, which also bypasses it for the new backup-code path
findings.body: The password verification is gated by `if (user.password && !credentials.totpCode)`, so any non-empty totpCode skips the password check entirely. The new backup-code branch (line 131) runs whenever credentials.backupCode is non-empty, regardless of totpCode. A request with a valid email, a valid backup code, and any non-empty totpCode (for example 'x') logs in without the password ever being verified. Backup codes are meant to replace only the second factor, but this turns them into a single-factor credential (email plus a 40-bit code). The same gap already exists for TOTP, but this PR adds a new route that depends on it. Password verification should not be skippable by supplying an unrelated second-factor field.

findings.title: Backup code consumption is an unlocked read-modify-write, allowing double use and restoration of spent codes
findings.body: The code is read and checked at lines 139-145, then the entire array is rewritten at line 149 with no transaction, lock, or conditional update. Two concurrent logins using the same code can both pass indexOf before either write lands, so one backup code can be spent twice. Concurrent logins with different codes also race: each writes back its own copy of the array, so the later write can restore a code the other request already nulled. Use an atomic compare-and-swap on the stored value (or a transaction with row locking) so that consumption is single-use.

findings.title: Users who reach 2FA via Google/SAML cannot use backup codes at all
findings.body: When 2FA is triggered after an OAuth/SAML sign-in (totpEmail set), the footer is ExternalTotpFooter, which only has a Cancel button, so the 'Lost access' toggle is never rendered. Even if the UI were reachable, authorize() in next-auth-options.ts (lines 113-115) throws ThirdPartyIdentityProviderEnabled for non-CAL users when totpCode is empty, so a backupCode-only submission is always rejected for these users. Users who sign in with Google or SAML and lose their authenticator therefore have no recovery path on the login page. Either wire backup codes into the external TOTP flow or state this limitation explicitly.

findings.title: Closing the backup-codes step via X/Escape/overlay skips the Close handler and loses the codes
findings.body: During DisplayBackupCodes the Dialog's onOpenChange is passed straight through, so the close X, Escape, and overlay click bypass the Close button's handler. By this point the enable request has already succeeded and 2FA is active on the server. onEnable() is never called, so the parent is not told 2FA is enabled, and the codes are discarded with no way to view them again. No regenerate endpoint exists in this PR. Route dismissals during this step through the same handler as the Close button, or block them until the codes have been acknowledged.

findings.title: tabIndex -1 on the password show/hide toggle removes it from keyboard navigation for every PasswordField
findings.body: This change is unrelated to backup codes and is not mentioned in the PR description, but it applies to every PasswordField in the app. tabIndex={-1} removes the visibility toggle from the Tab order, so keyboard-only users can no longer reveal a password they typed. The button has only an sr-only label, so it is effectively unreachable without a pointer. This is an accessibility regression. If the goal was only to skip the toggle on the login form, handle it at that call site instead.

findings.title: type="password" passed to PasswordField overrides its computed type, so the show/hide toggle does nothing
findings.body: PasswordField renders type={isPasswordVisible ? 'text' : 'password'} and then spreads {...props} afterward. The type='password' passed here wins, so the input never switches to text. Clicking the eye toggle changes the icon and label but the value stays hidden. This was previously a plain TextField; the swap introduces a dead control on the enable-2FA password step. Drop the explicit type prop.

findings.title: Non-string backupCode from JSON body throws an unhandled TypeError
findings.body: req.body.backupCode is taken from a JSON body without type checking. Any truthy non-string value (number, object, array) makes .replaceAll throw, which escapes the handler as an unhandled exception and returns a 500 instead of a JSON error. Check typeof req.body.backupCode === 'string' before normalizing it.

findings.title: missing_backup_codes tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such action exists
findings.body: The message says 'No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings.' No UI in this PR generates codes outside the initial setup, and the setup endpoint refuses to run once 2FA is enabled. Users who enabled 2FA before this change (backupCodes null) are shown this message on login and sent to a screen where they cannot act. Their only path is disabling 2FA with a TOTP code and re-enabling it. Reword the message or add a regenerate action.

findings.title: Enable test asserts on a switch behind the open backup-codes dialog, with a known-vacuous assertion left in place
findings.body: The PR adds a FIXME stating that this assertion 'passes even when switch is not checked'. The enable test also never closes the backup-codes dialog that now sits on top of the page, so the switch is checked behind the modal. The assertion is therefore weak and knowingly so. Close the dialog and assert data-state='checked' as the disable test does, rather than shipping a check the author has already identified as not validating anything.

findings.title: No test covers logging in with a backup code, the core new behavior
findings.body: The TODO defers backup-code login testing, but this is the main user-facing addition of the PR (the 'Lost access' flow). Nothing exercises the authorize() backup-code branch, the consumption of a code, rejection of reuse, or the new error messages. The disable-endpoint backup path is also untested. At minimum, add an e2e test that logs in with a code, confirms it is accepted once, and confirms reuse is rejected.

findings.title: Copy button shows success toast without awaiting or handling clipboard failure
findings.body: navigator.clipboard.writeText returns a promise that is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast fires unconditionally. On insecure origins or when permission is denied, the write fails (or navigator.clipboard is undefined and throws), yet the user is told 'Backup codes copied!'. Await the promise and show an error toast on failure.

findings.title: Plaintext backup codes and blob URL persist in component state after the dialog closes
findings.body: resetState() clears password and step but not backupCodes or backupCodesUrl. After the dialog is closed, the plaintext recovery codes stay in React state, and the blob URL that encodes them is never revoked on close (it is only revoked on the next setup call). Clear the codes and revoke the URL when the dialog closes.

findings.title: Backup codes stored reversibly instead of hashed
findings.body: Backup codes are stored with symmetricEncrypt, so anyone holding CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY, or a DB dump together with that key, can recover every unused code and log in as the user. These codes are bearer secrets. Because they are random and high-entropy, a one-way hash (for example SHA-256 with a comparison on the submitted code) would suffice and remove this exposure. Severity is low because the same key already protects TOTP secrets.
